title: Two Thoughts on the Transmission of Monetary Policy (+ Q&A)
summary: In the post-speech Q&A, Waller reaffirmed his May (Frankfurt) hawkish pivot: 'those risks have completely flipped around now,' with the labor market stabilizing and inflation 'taking off,' so — after a year of advocating cuts on labor-market grounds — he now leans toward getting inflation back to 2% faster. He reiterated a firm commitment to the 2% target (reframing Warsh's 'recommit' as merely 'reaffirm'), said he personally prefers a 1.5–2% range but that changing the target now would not be credible, and stressed communicating a well-defined reaction function over forward guidance. On fiscal dominance he was emphatic on Fed independence: the FOMC will raise rates when needed and will not hold them down to cheapen government financing. (The prepared remarks were a methodological talk on transmission and forward guidance with no monetary-policy stance and are left unscored; this classification reflects the Q&A only.)

key_quotes.quote: But as I gave a speech back in May in Frankfurt, those risks have completely flipped around now. Labor market seems to be stabilizing in the U.S. Inflation has been taking off. So then that changes how you might want to think about policy.
key_quotes.context: Q&A: reaffirms the May hawkish pivot — labor stabilizing, inflation accelerating, mandate risk now on the inflation side.

key_quotes.quote: We've had inflation above target for five years. And so one of the issues is, yes, we'll get back to 2%. It's just a question of when. So possibly you're committing to saying we're going to get there faster... but maybe we will now.
key_quotes.context: Q&A: five years above target and a willingness to get back to 2% faster now — firmer inflation conviction.

key_quotes.quote: So a year ago I was advocating for rate cuts because the labor market was not looking good. So I was willing to tolerate a longer movement back to our 2% target based on the labor market.
key_quotes.context: Q&A: dual-mandate framing that has now flipped — last year labor justified cuts, now the balance has shifted to inflation.

key_quotes.quote: My very first speech I ever gave as a governor was saying, when it comes time to raise rates, we will do it. We will not sit there and hold rates to keep the financing costs of the U.S. government low.
key_quotes.context: Q&A on fiscal dominance: emphatic Fed independence — will raise rates regardless of government financing costs.
